instruction:
You are interviewing a shop about a job they already do, until the procedure is unambiguous enough that two different technicians working alone would produce the same record. Ask about ONE thing per turn, in their language, never in the vocabulary of forms. Compile only when nothing material is still unstated: every step has a reason someone would accept, every field has an acceptance rule that can actually be applied to what comes back, and a bound that came from the shop rather than from you. Inventing a tolerance is the one thing you must never do — a figure nobody stated must not appear in what you compile. A shop that does not know one will not know it when asked again: take the first 'I don't know' as final, keep it in unresolved if it matters, and move on. Your turns are few. Spend them on the figures that decide whether the job passed, never on detail beneath them.

Return JSON with these fields:
- mode (one of ask | compile, required): ask while anything material is unstated. compile once the procedure would run unambiguously.
- question (string, null when it does not apply): Required when mode is ask. One question about one thing, phrased for a mechanic, not a form designer. Never a list, never a preamble, never a restatement of what they just told you, and never one they have already said they cannot answer.
- asks_about (one of scope | sequence | tolerance | evidence | failure | authority | parts | safety, null when it does not apply): Which class of unknown this question closes. Required when mode is ask.
- unresolved (array, required): Everything you still do not know that would change the compiled procedure. Complete every turn, not only what you just asked about. Empty is the only condition under which you may compile.
- understanding (string, required): What you now believe the job is, in two sentences. Written every turn so the shop can correct you early rather than at the end.
- draft (object, null when it does not apply): Required when mode is compile. The procedure as it would run tomorrow.

output.understanding: The job is to replace the brake fluid on a bicycle or e-bike, ensuring the correct fluid type is used and the system is free of air and leaks. We verify this by checking the stamped fluid type, documenting the drained fluid, and confirming a rock-solid lever feel and leak-free fittings.

draft.title: Brake Fluid Replacement and Bleed
disqualifiers: Brake lever feels squishy or pulls to the handlebar
releases: Safe to ride in city traffic and on gravel

steps.title: Identify Fluid Type
steps.explanation: Using the wrong fluid (such as putting DOT in a mineral oil brake) swells the seals and completely ruins the brakes within a week.

fields.prompt: Take a photo of the fluid type stamp on the brake lever body or reservoir cap.
fields.acceptance_description: The stamped fluid type (MINERAL OIL or DOT) must be clearly legible.
fields.guidance: Locate the text stamped on the lever body or reservoir cap. Ensure the photo is in focus and the text is readable.

steps.title: Bleed Brakes per Manufacturer Spec
steps.explanation: Bleeding must follow the specific brake manufacturer's procedure to ensure all air is purged and pads/rotors are not contaminated.

fields.prompt: Confirm you have looked up and followed the official bleeding and pad-protection procedure for the brake brand stamped on the lever.
fields.guidance: Refer to the official manual for the specific brand of brakes on your bike to protect pads and run the fluid correctly.

steps.title: Document Drained Fluid
steps.explanation: Verifies that the old fluid has been fully replaced.

fields.prompt: Take a photo of the old brake fluid drained from the system.
fields.acceptance_description: The drained fluid in a container, showing it has been removed from the system.
fields.guidance: Capture the old fluid in your bleed bucket or syringe to document the flush.

steps.title: Verify Lever Feel
steps.explanation: A squishy lever or one that pulls to the bar indicates air in the system, which can cause brake failure in traffic.

fields.prompt: Squeeze the brake lever as hard as you can. How does it feel?
choices: Rock solid and does not pull back to the handlebar
Squishy or pulls all the way to the handlebar
fields.acceptance_target: Rock solid and does not pull back to the handlebar
fields.guidance: The lever must feel completely firm and stop well before touching the handlebar grip.

steps.title: Check for Leaks
steps.explanation: Any slow leak or weeping will lead to loss of braking power and potential failure.

fields.prompt: Inspect all hoses, fittings, and bleed ports. Is there any fluid weeping?
fields.guidance: Wipe down all fittings and check closely. Any sign of wetness or weeping is a failure.
